utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're at the foot of page 5 of the summary, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we put tab 3 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the coordination group of which you've spoken also involved in assisting in the establishment and organisation of the Krajina Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the coordination group did not engage in the formation of the Territorial Defence, but it did engage in providing assistance to the TO staff in organising certain structures and units of the Territorial Defence, such as the TO brigades in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Furthermore, we also assisted them in organising the zonal staffs of the Territorial Defence and the actual staff of the SAO Krajina. We helped them in constituting the units out of the existing lower-level units and manpower that they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just looking at the chart, tab 3, and at the orange colour at the bottom, show what that reveals of this part of the coordination office's work.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've just drawn the orange lines which reflect that you communicated with the General Staff of the JNA administration, JNA organisation administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that orders on organisation and structure then would have gone out from that body to the Krajina Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the administration for organisation and formation of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at tab 9. Overhead projector, page 1. Order on organisational formational changes in the units of Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska. And then to page 2, which we have a document dated after your period of office, General, 2nd of March, 1992. Federal Secretariat for National Defence to the zone command of the Territorial Defence in Glina. "Please find enclosed order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence." Third page, please. State secret 2nd of February 1992 from the Federal Secretary for National Defence. The order organisational formational changes, item 1: "Establish General Staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Srpska Krajina ..." Does this documentation reflect, although after your time, the work of the coordination office in assisting the organisation and structure of the Territorial Defence in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, only this is a modification of what preceded it, because in this period of time, the Republic of Srpska Krajina had been inaugurated. In the meantime, it had -- it was the Serbian Autonomous Region. Now it became the republic and the staff was adjusted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 3 again, please. Financial issues. Top of the chart. Can you summarise, please, the role of the coordination office in financial issues? We can see it in green to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us what the coordination office did so far as finances are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, Mr. Prosecutor, that yesterday I mentioned that the TO brigades were financed within the framework of the command of the corps and operative groups when they were subordinated to them or, rather, when they were integrated within their system. They were exempted from the command of the TO staff. When they were not directly under their command, then financially they relied on their own Krajina staff. However, about two-thirds of the members of the TO were outside the brigades. They were members of lower-level units. And since the monetary and fiscal system had collapsed over there, the people who were in the Krajina Territorial Defence did not receive salaries or any financial remuneration, and these were mostly reservists with families who had no livelihood. And then from the SAO Krajina staff, they appealed to us that we intervene with the government of Serbia and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence for a lump sum to be paid out to them, a one-time payment within reasonable limits. We requested that the staff tell us the exact numerical strength in categories; soldiers and non-commissioned officers and officers, because their remuneration varied. Once they did that, my officers in the coordination group went to the financial administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and set out the situation to them. And the financial body, the financial officer in the Defence Ministry, that is a permanent employee, contacted the Ministry for Finance and the budget in the Republic of Serbia. Then these two financial officials of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and in the government of Serbia agreed on how they would contribute, each in providing financial assistance in accordance to the request we had received. I didn't interfere any further with that because this was carried out by the officials in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You only addressed or were aware of contacts being made with the financial administration of the SSNO, but could that sector of the SSNO have made the decision on its own or must it have gone to the highest level for the decision to be approved?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to go to a higher level. The head of the administration for finance and the budget could not decide such a matter on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise within the Ministry of Finance for the Republic of Serbia, could that decision have been made without intervention of or approval by the Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they couldn't have without the approval of the government. And yesterday we saw a document - I can't remember the date - in which the Defence Ministry is addressing itself to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You only, because of the period of your office, you only know of the one payment, but the problem, so far as you could see, was that a problem that would inevitably continue and require further solution?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it forecast within your department or your office that a regular payment system would have to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assumed so, but this was beyond our terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 10, please. One month after your termination of office, a document from the 2nd Military District Command, dated the 20th of January, from them to the 622nd Motorised Brigade, reading: "In dispatch with above mentioned mark and date, you requested explanation about the rights of families of killed members of Territorial Defence on the area of Croatia ..." And then at the bottom of the block of text, just above Colonel General Kukanja's signature: "Considering that you've sent the marked dispatch to personal administration of the SSNO, it's to be expected that the problems will be seen at the whole and that the just solution will be found. We think families of killed Territorial Defence members on the territory of the Republic of Croatia should be entitled to all rights as well as the persons from the reserve forces units and the JNA institutions." Does this reflect the way in which financial responsibility for those engaged in the territory of Croatia was shouldered?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The late General Kukanja, commander of the 2nd Military District - he died last year - he provides here an explanation in response to a request from below what his position is. And because it is addressed to the personnel administration, he says that he expects that a unified solution would be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 11, please. Again a month or five weeks or so after the end of office but nevertheless you can help us with it. From the Republic of Serb Krajina's Ministry of Interior to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia, in particular to Minister Sokolovic, a letter signed by Milan Martic, the last paragraph of which reads: "I inform you that there is a --" "I inform you that there is an amount of 380 million dinars in the SDK in Glina," which is the federal bookkeeping service, I think, if we look at the paragraph above. "These resources were earlier deposited for the Territorial Defence, but since the major part of the defence, the defenders, that is, were financed from the army budget, the above-mentioned resources have not been spent for some time. We ask you to influence that these resources be transferred to the account of the Ministry of the Interior of RSK." So how does this relate to the Coordination Group? Does this reflect the activities of the Coordination Group in transferring money?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain. The social accounting service, or the SDK, in Glina, in Banja Luka, in Knin, and I can't remember where it was based for the Eastern Slavonia, received money which had been agreed on between the financial bodies of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. And this statement by Mr. Martic that certain funds had mostly been provided by the JNA I don't think is quite correct and that what is involved is only inefficiency or errors in the work of the bodies of the Territorial Defence of that particular zone which didn't go to the SDK, withdraw the money from it and distribute the funds to its members. But otherwise, it did affect us, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The money had come from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the SSNO and Serbia. And now what the ratio was between the two, I don't know, but I do know that both participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same general period, 8th of February, 1992. Going to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina for the territories of Knin and Lika, coming from the Republic of Serbia's Ministry of Defence and over the signature of Minister Lieutenant-Colonel General Marko Njegovanovic. The bottom paragraph reads --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. "The resources are transferred to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence for the territory of Knin and Lika in the amount of 500.000 dinars for the purchase of building material ..." Does this, although comparatively modest in amount, nevertheless match the system of coordination of office work on finance?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does match. And this is actually evidence that these obligations continued to be fulfilled. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 3, please, on the overhead projector. In this chart, General, which you prepared or assisted in preparing, we see at the bottom right-hand corner, right at the bottom of the -- thank you very much. We see in the little black and white block reference to other tasks which haven't been presented diagrammatically, one of which was the preparation for the arrival of United Nations peace forces. In a couple of sentences, please, the function of the coordination office in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, my offices were not involved in that with the exception of myself, as far as I can recollect, and of course the Minister of Defence. Upon instructions from the Minister, I went to the General Staff of the JNA, to the General headquarters, and I had a briefing there with the late Major General Slavko Jovic. He also died. General Slavko Jovic, during the Iran-Iraq conflict, was a member of the contingent of international peace forces, and for a cessation of hostilities there, and according to assessments at the time, he had a wealth of experience in the area. I presented to General Jovic the situation such as it was in Krajina as far as I was familiar with it, the rough distribution of forces and division of the territory and so on. And then he, knowing Mr. Marrack Goulding personally from the period I just mentioned, provided very brief instructions as to how steps -- which steps should be taken in Croatia or in Krajina to receive the international forces. As far as I remember, though I didn't -- haven't kept the notes, there were three points that were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to deal with this very briefly. Was this in November of 1991, and did you thereafter meet representatives of Serb Autonomous Region's government such as Babic, Hadzic and Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally, in the presence of the minister, explained to them the instructions given to me by General Jovic as to what should be done in Krajina in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was Babic's attitude towards the mandate of the forces that was explained?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that he wasn't enthusiastic about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his concern about what the JNA might do if he didn't accept the --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key cause of his concern at the time, fully understanding the function of the forces and their duties there, was that everything would be okay but what if the Croatian forces, the National Guards or their army, as it was called, launch an all-out offensive and Krajina had, in the meantime, demobilised its Territorial Defence? What then would happen to their autonomy, independence, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have any concerns about what the JNA would or wouldn't do?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he linked that to his concern that they would be left to fend for themselves as the JNA would have to pull out from Knin, the 9th Corps, so that they would have no one to rely on. So that was his main concern, judging by the conversations we had at the time and as far as I can remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the belief or understanding on the part of the officers of the JNA as to the JNA's obligations to Serbs in the United Nations Protected Areas?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot mention a specific document or a meeting or any particular decision, but I do know that communicating with the officers and generals, it was said that the Yugoslav People's Army was ready should such an attempt be made by the Croatian side to come to their help and to protect them and not to allow the war to flare up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next topic, very briefly: Volunteers. I don't think the coordination office dealt directly with the administration of volunteers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for officers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 23rd of August of 1991, did the government of Serbia order a -- issue an enlistment order for volunteers into the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but may I make a correction? It's not mobilisation, because that makes it obligatory, but, rather, enlistment of those who volunteer. So it's admission of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 13th of September of 1991, by an instruction of the SSNO, was there a further order?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This instruction dealt with the acceptance of volunteers into JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an order banning political parties within the armed forces on the 8th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. This order was taken precisely because of the earlier paramilitary forces which had mainly been formed by certain parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the object of these orders, or one of the objects of these orders would have been to have brought to an end political parties having paramilitary organisations or military organisations. Do you know one way or another whether these decisions were fully implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may first make a comment. There was another order, issued by the Presidency of the SFRY, on the obligation for the volunteers who were already within the armed forces to be included in regular units of the TO and the JNA, that they cannot exist in any other form, that they even had to be disbanded, et cetera. But in order to your question, I think that this was not fully implemented as subsequent conflicts revealed later on as I was able to follow from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the document we can now look at, tab 13, please, which is dated the 10th of December. And if we'd simply go to the third page of this. That's it. Thank you very much. This is a decree on the registration of volunteers which regulates -- Article 1 regulates the registration of volunteers; the reinforcement of JNA, people's army, with volunteers is carried out in accordance with the regulations. At the foot of this page sets out Article 3, and: "The registration of volunteers in Territorial Defence is carried out in wartime, in the case of immediate danger of war and state of emergency, in order to fill units, headquarters, and institutions of Territorial Defence." I was wrong when I said December. If you'd turn over three pages, you come to the date, which is the 14th of August, 1991. Thank you very much. Is this the order you were speaking of, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order issued by the government of Serbia. It was signed by the vice-president, Nikola Stanic, published in the Official Gazette of Serbia on the 23rd of August --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any of those -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and issued -- pardon? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I interrupted you. But implementation required declaration of one of the states, war and so on. Do you know if it was implemented in that way or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part it was, but imminent danger of war was declared later, on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 14. I don't think we need necessarily look at it. It's the 13th of September order. To save time, it's there. Perhaps it could be counted as produced, in the absence of any objection, and we'll move on to the next topic. General, I want you to help us, please, with the Ministry of Defence briefly, Tomislav Simovic. Did you meet him occasionally, although he was always rather busy?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he receive reports about what your group was learning from the Krajina field operations and what it was learning about the needs of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the time he had available, because he often had to attend meetings of the government, we would meet, as a rule, two or three times a week, because his office was in another part of town. I would come to his office, telling him that there were certain things I had to inform him about, or he would call me to come to his office and give him information and brief him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you also speak to, and I suppose, brief his deputy, Brana Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the absence of the Minister of Defence if there was an urgent matter that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you deal with other people who you worked with, including Colonel Mladenko Kovacevic, and a civilian called Hristoljub Cekic, but in addition to those two, there was Dobrila Gajic-Glisic, who was Simovic's chef de cabinet and she was in charge of all meetings with the Serbian government, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning now to the accused, you were not present, I think, at any meetings between Minister Simovic and the accused.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't present at any meetings, and I did not see or hear Mr. Milosevic for almost 15 years, including in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Simovic tell you whether he'd had any meetings with the accused about matters related to the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did say things, but there are some things that I think we should not discuss openly, in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into closed session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Private session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Djordjevic, dealing with your talks with Mr. Simovic, the minister, did he ever let you know one way or another whether the accused was aware of the Coordination Group and its activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told very clearly that he had met the president of Serbia and probably some details about what we were doing, but I don't know what they talked about in detail specifically except that he briefed the president that such a group existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your discussions with the minister and from what was talked about in your department, did you form a view as to whether the accused had a close or less close relationship with the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, than with the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely, what it was -- he was closer to the MUP than the Ministry of Defence. That was your judgement?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Sokolovic and Mr. Milosevic knew each other. They went a long way back. They had worked together in the League of Communists and maybe there was something else behind it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Momcilo Perisic when he was chief of the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when he was a chief, I met him twice. On one occasion when there was a reception on the occasion of the Day of the Army in the army club when we from the Association of Military Pensioners were also invited. This was a social organisation. And the other occasion was when he briefed retired generals and admirals in Topcider on current issues concerning the organisation of the J -- of the Yugoslav army, financial problems, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was something said at one of those meetings, perhaps the second one, about the comparative size of the budget of Serbia and the budget of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, I think his name was, his assistant, since General Perisic only announced what the topic would be, he informed us. And there was another general there who was probably in charge of logistics. When they completed their presentation, General Perisic threw the floor open for questions and asked if there were any proposals or suggestions concerning the topic that had been discussed. A few of us took the floor. I put some questions about the funding of the army of Yugoslavia. And in this plenary discussion among retired generals, I asked the following: "General, all of us can see through the media what the budget of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is and what the budget of the Republic of Serbia is. It is common knowledge that most of the funds from the budget of Yugoslavia go to fund the army, because that's what the structure of the budget was then and still is. It is also common knowledge that the Ministry of the Interior uses most of these funds. If we compare these two budgets, I can't say what the figures are now, we can see that far more funds are allocated to the police than to the army. Furthermore, we are all aware of the fact that the police carries only light weapons and that the army has heavy weapons - guns, tanks, ships, planes, and so on - and that the needs for funding cannot be compared. Besides this, in spite of the embargo and the difficult financial situation of Yugoslavia, the police are given three new uniforms, an official uniform, and so on, while the army cannot even get new insignia and buttons. What does this mean?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made this statement to --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me add something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, listen, General. Just -- would you be guided by the Prosecutor, please, because time is short, and he will know what's relevant to this case, which is what we need to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's very helpful, General, what you've been telling us, and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. picture you're painting is a very full one. Did you form a view yourself about what the accused was doing with his police and into what form of guard he was converting them?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they were becoming the praetorian guard, which is no longer the case today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you made these observations to Perisic, what was his reaction to you on behalf of the authorities or speaking on --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, his reaction was as follows: "General Djordjevic, don't say those things. That's what the opposition is saying nowadays."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we part from this, can you just help me with a matter of detail: Who was the Minister of Finance at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two short topics, General, and then I'm done. The coordination office, did it receive information about criminal behaviour of paramilitary groups, in particular from Milan Paspalj and Dusan Kasum?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did get some very general information, such as there were certain incidents, and this all referred to the period of July, August, September. There was a man who had been a partisan from the Krajina who would come to our office and who spoke of individual incidents such as operation Cadet or Opel, I don't know what he called it. He said that a paramilitary unit had attacked a village - I don't know what village - and that the group leader said the best fighter will get a car because there is a new car in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a report of an attack on an ethnically mixed village of Lika -- in Lika, I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special report. I gleaned this from the conversations I'd had with the president of the Assembly, the Chief of Staff, and other people. But we sent on information in a general way to the General Staff that such things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So notice went to the General Staff. Did it go to the minister, information of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister was aware of this, and he responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he issue a warning?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He issued an oral warning to the president of the SAO Krajina, Mr. Babic, and the commander of the TO of the SAO Krajina, and said that if such things happened, they would have to be dealt with by the courts that had been set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 15, please. Last exhibit. Order of the 14th of October of 1991 by Blagoje Adzic, ordering JNA units to ensure international humanitarian law regulations are observed, to prevent looting, not to attack cultural goods. Item 4, to submit breaches to the legal organs. This reflects a recognition of the existence of crimes having been committed, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Final point. Totally different topic. Matter of detail. On the 26th of July of 1991, when the problems with Slovenia were at a critical stage, were you aware of whether there was any preparation to launch an airstrike against Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the generals knew that preparations were under way for an airstrike because the conclusion had been reached that the Slovenian side was not complying with the agreement that had been reached on the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say preparations were under way, what quantity of aircraft are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know officially, but I heard from a friend in the air force that they had a brigade ready with weapons but then they gave up the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A brigade, is that sometimes, in air force terms, called a wing?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was misinterpreted. This is "wing" in Serbia, but that is a regiment or a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, these planes were on a state of readiness to go and bomb Ljubljana, and this is the sort of state of preparedness that should be reflected by documentation still available to the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's how it should have been, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- that's -- this will prove to be an example of the ability of the authorities to respond to our now targeted requests, or another targeted request. We'll seek those documents immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the SFRY Prime Minister Ante Markovic go to Ljubljana in an effort to prevent that attack, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was publicly reported that Mr. Markovic went there to have talks with Mr. Kucan, the president of Slovenia, and also to be some sort of guarantee by his person that there would be no such attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the attack didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, two administrative matters which we can deal with very briefly. The first is this, while we have it in mind: You provided a chart of witnesses or times last week to Judge Kwon and I when we were sitting alone. I don't think one was provided to Judge Robinson. Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In due course. Together with, I think -- I'm not sure it was ever filed with the Registry, your observations. I've forgotten what it was called, but you produced a document on the same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We produced a chart, a visual aid. I don't think I produced any speaking notes. I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I can remember the chart, and we can provide that if a copy didn't go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There was a -- there was a list of remaining witnesses, but it may be that that was filed anyway. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a list of witnesses which came with, I think, a letter to the Registrar, Mr. Holthuis, and the only other document was the visual aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind but certainly the visual aid should be supplied, if you would. The other matter concerns this: That we ought to try and make progress with the Rule 92 bis witnesses for Croatia, which we made a start on but haven't got very far. What may be convenient is to find some time towards the end of the week, an hour or so, and try and get through some more. That will require, really, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. I don't know if she's here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She is here. It would be particularly convenient to deal with it at the end of the week. I shan't be here and we may have a witness gap problem. I very much hope not, but we already considered this morning raising 92 bis issues on Thursday or Friday. The amici, I know, have looked for a longer time period to deal with it but we would press them to be in a position to deal with them by Thursday or Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want -- we've got the witness here, I don't want to enter into a lengthy discussion. What I'm simply asking is that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is present later in the morning, and we can go through, as it were, the next tranche of witnesses that we'll deal with so that everybody can have them prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's only the Dokmanovic transcript witness statements that I'm waiting for. But as soon as I have them, I can finish what I've already done in draft within two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can tell you what I had in mind: Moving off Vukovar and going on to Dubrovnik and dealing with those witnesses at the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can deal with all those 92 bis ones that were filed in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And leaving the Vukovar transcripts to next week or so when we've all had more time with them. Yes. Well, if she could be present later we could discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You want her later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order to prepare for later in the week. Certainly. I would use that opportunity to mention a couple of administrative things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll try to do that towards the end of the morning, or after this witness. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, at the beginning of your statement, you speak of the factors that -- or the events that preceded the armed conflicts in the territory of Croatia and as far as I was able to note, you mentioned first paramilitary formations; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't, Mr. Milosevic. Your Honours, I divided the introductory part of my statement into two; first the political factors and, secondly, the military factors that led up to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the military factors now. If we're talking about military factors, then is what I say right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is taken out of context. If you are referring to paramilitary organisations in Slovenia and Croatia, which were legitimate but illegal, illegal in the sense that they were in contravention of the federal law, then you're right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is the misunderstanding then?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is generalised, because the Serbs also had paramilitary forces which were neither legitimate nor legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the things that I assume you're very well acquainted with. Do you know that those first paramilitary formations were those of Croatia? That is the first time we heard of such things. Then we heard of the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, and various foreign mercenaries who were coming. Do you know anything about that? Wasn't that the beginning of the conflict in Yugoslavia, viewing it from the military aspect?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the engagement of the Yugoslav People's Army, it was put in a situation to get involved in the conflicts because it was primarily that it was attacked first in Slovenia and then intensively and on a large scale in Croatia. But when we come to events in the SAO Krajina, then that's a different topic, when we're talking about paramilitary formations. The JNA was still there, a buffer, up until the time when I got involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, what was the target of attack by all those paramilitary formations that were formed in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier for me to answer what was not targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please try and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've written all that in my statement, but I'll repeat that. There were attacks against the families, military personnel, kidnapping, arrests, murders, harassment of various kinds. Then cutting off water, electricity, heating for military barracks. Then it escalated into putting up barricades in front of the entrance to barracks. Then even machine-gun nests and then it climaxed with physical attacks against JNA barracks in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, General, the Serbian population in Croatia, was it jeopardised by those paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially yes and partially no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were the Serbs forced to organise themselves in their defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started to organise themselves when members of the National Guards Corps and special units of the Croatian MUP tried by force to disarm certain police stations in Knin, Glina, Pakrac - I can't remember all those details - and the Serbs resisted this. And I think it is clearly stated over there that for the Serbs, the symbol of the chequerboard, the chequerboard symbol meant something quite different to them. It reminded them of events of the Second World War, of Pavlic's Ustasha state, and so on, and this logically led up to conflict, sporadic incidents. But when these became more large scale, then at the state level, at the level of the Federal Secretariat a decision was taken to establish a buffer zone to separate these conflicting groups; village guards, MUP, Croatian patrols and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. That is not in dispute. But my question is: Were the Serbs forced to self-organise because they were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that the civil war in Yugoslavia - this is on page 1 of your statement - led to a monoethnic state with the exception of Serbian Macedonia. You speak about that in your statement. And tell me, how did these Yugoslav republics manage to become monoethnic in nature? How did they become monoethnic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that is speaking too strictly, because in Slovenia there were about a hundred or 150.000 people of a different ethnicity. But they had become monoethnic over a period of decades. But now in the 1990s, by the secession of Slovenia, Croatia, and later on Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this process is common knowledge. Now, why this happened, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs lived in Croatia according to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. Around 270.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirteen per cent of the population of Croatia, so I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the exact figure, but that doesn't matter. How did Croatia become a monoethnic state?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serbs were expelled after the Storm campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear, because you were involved during the period that you're testifying about but also earlier, as a citizen, were you, as a senior officer in the JNA earlier on, had you ever heard, while the war was being waged in Croatia and also in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had you ever heard that the authorities in Serbia had expelled in any way a member of any ethnic minority?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities did not, but some did, and the authorities didn't intervene with enough resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did this, then? Who expelled people?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vice-Premier of the government, as he used to be, and now a colleague of yours detained here in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that the authorities did not intervene energetically and did not protect each and every citizen.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak in absolute terms and say every citizen, but what was quite evident was that the Croats were being expelled from Srem. I'm not saying that they were killed but they were being harassed in various ways. And the Serbian authorities kept silent about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no information as to how the authorities protected members of other ethnic groups where they were in jeopardy. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that police patrols were reinforced and a system of control intensified. I know that. But when a system of fear developed among those who were put in those -- in that position by those who were bringing pressure to bear on them and that were harassing them, all that was too late. But I'm not talking in general terms about the attitude of the Serbian authorities towards any particular ethnic group in Serbia. I'm just talking about these specific cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that all the cases which the police in those days intervened to prevent were actually committed by refugees from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and not by citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, do you believe that secession from the federal state, first by Slovenia and then by Croatia, was the main cause of the break-up of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with a yes or no. I can answer it in several sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: De jure, Slovenia and Croatia violated the existing system of reaching agreement about such matters as the integrity of the country, separation, independence, and so on, whatever you like to call them. They did not respect that system. In Dr. Drnovsek's book entitled "Moja Resnica" in Slovenian, or "My Truth," he himself acknowledges this that Slovenia did not respect the procedure envisaged by the federal constitution, the laws, et cetera. However, at the same time, he justifies this by saying that with respect to the other side, let's say the Serbian side, a common language could not be found about the proposals that were coming from Slovenia in those days. He doesn't talk about Croatia. And that is true too. But, Mr. Milosevic, it is also true that you and the leadership of the country at the time and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence - and I'm talking about the leadership - assisted this process, in speeding up this process, and you were not sufficiently responsible statesmen to find a solution modelled on the separation between the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not start a debate about that Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you ask him these questions. Whether they're relevant or not, we haven't stopped you. You don't like the answer, so you stop him. Let him finish. Now, General, is there anything you want to add to what you've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Your Honours, if I may use not my own personal evidence but a book that has been tendered here as a document of some kind -- I don't know exactly what kind, a book by Dr. Borisav Jovic, the closest associate of Mr. Milosevic. Page 160, pages 243, 257, 347, I repeat. On those pages alone, Mr. Boro Jovic gives the real truth, opinions, and assessments of all these questions. De jure it is the Slovenes and Croats who are at fault - I mean their leaderships - and de facto something quite different. So let Mr. Milosevic read this so I don't need to quote what is said on those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, in your statement you speak about this. I understand your position. But in your statement, you say that the new Croatian authorities introduced new state symbols, coat of arms, flag, et cetera. Do you know that up until then, up until the amendment to the constitution in Croatia, the Serb people were treated in the constitutional sense as a constituent people and then were thrown out of the constitution? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And that was one of the causes for the rebellion of the Serbs in Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that this resurrected fascism and Ustasha Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. policies is something that the authorities were to blame for and Serbia was to blame for?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. But until all that happened, there were no reasonable steps taken or attempts for you in the leadership to come to some sort of an agreement. There were even malicious attitudes towards what was allegedly in preparation in Slovenia and Macedonia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think, General, that you know full well that we had no reason to be in conflict with the Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peoples did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nor the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the leadership of Serbia was not even informed about the intervention of the army in Slovenia, which was the idea upheld by the then Federal Prime Minister Ante Markovic and his bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea of Mr. Markovic, in order to protect legality and the functioning of the customs system, the frontier services and the rest was well-intentioned. However, the decision that he signed as the Federal Prime Minister, that was president of the government then called the Federal Executive Council, was exhorted from him. What Mr. Markovic had proposed to the Slovenes the Slovenes did not accept. And on the other hand, he was under pressure from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and from several people in the federal authorities, the Presidency, et cetera. And then such a decision was taken which was a compromise. Let me call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did Serbia have to do with that? Did Serbia have anything to do with that? According to your own knowledge, your knowledge today and everything you knew from before.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, and I repeat from the book of your personal friend Mr. Borisav Jovic, you had agreed -- discussed with him on the 27th of June, 1990, how to get rid of Slovenia, how to cut it off overnight. Slovenia and half of Croatia. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we can ask Jovic about his book. You don't need to explain his book. But I am asking you about your own knowledge and not about Jovic's book. You're not testifying about Jovic's book here.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my own knowledge, the Republic of Slovenia advocated an asymmetrical federation, the Republic of Croatia a confederation, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia favoured some kind of a loose federation. However, the Serbian side - but allow me - I personally also was in favour of a federation of a firm country, but that -- what we wish is one thing and when we come to a solution that would avoid war is another. But that is the politicians that are responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Without any doubt. The politicians bear the greatest responsibility. But when you mention a compromise solution advocated by Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you're referring to that well-known formula Izetbegovic-Gligorov.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that Serbia accepted the solution that they proposed, Izetbegovic, Gligorov? This was published in all the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say yes then I must add something else that I know and it's better for us not to talk about that. I think we're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Djordjevic. When discussing the responsibility of politicians, tell me, how was the Yugoslav crisis affected by the support of Germany and some other external factors for the secession of Croatia to be precise?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally destructively, as is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what assistance was provided to Croatia apart from political support and the urgent recognition which took place before political problems had been solved?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they received instructors from Germany, that descendants of the Ustasha emigres came back to the country as well as various mercenaries, that they obtained weapons secretly from Hungary and by ship from other places. I know all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know something about the material assistance that these secessionists in Croatia received and the paramilitary units in Croatia and the regime received?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About 150 or 200 million dollars from somewhere. I don't know whether it was Germany or the USA or Austria but I know it was from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because the opposite side here has been asking you about 500.000 dinars given by Serbs to help Serbs. So I wanted to clarify whether you knew something about this assistance provided by Germans and from other countries. Let's not go into discussion of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other countries now. Tell me what you know about who was in the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this. Should I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Democratic Union. The party that won the elections in 1990. And later on, this was legalised by the parliament which transformed these people into the National Guard of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the ruling party for the first time after World War II was the first party to arm its members, I don't know if anything like this occurred between World War II and this phenomenon in Croatia, after the political rhetoric and the constitutional changes, was this also a decisive factor that caused the Serbs to organise themselves and organise their defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of the major factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you are a general, a very high-ranking general, tell me, do you remember how many barracks were attacked and how many officers and soldiers were killed in the first wave of violence that erupted on the territory of Croatia in an attempt to achieve secession?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have forgotten the figures, but what is important is that not a single barracks or a single military facility in Croatia was not attacked. So that's a full reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Do you know that there were -- that there were plans to liquidate JNA officers and to retaliate against their families?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this was a general practice?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the National Guard Corps was in fact an anti-Yugoslav and especially anti-Serb formation, armed formation?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's well known. But all extreme nationalist parties were the same, more or less, in other parts of the country as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that the Serbs engaged in civil disobedience, is it true that they were disobedient to an illegally established state, and at the same time obedient to a country where for decades they had realised their rights and been respected?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Croatia was legally established at the elections, but it became independent illegally. These are two separate matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about a state.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did the Federal Secretariat for National Defence respond to all these events?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted from what General Blagoje Adzic, the Chief of the General Staff said when he briefed us in July 1991: "With deep concern." That's the answer to your question. And another thing. The Federal Secretariat had a full picture of the events, and they also had evaluation -- an evaluation of the prospects for the future and what might happen. It wasn't fortune-telling, it was an evaluation of possible future events. Excuse me. The constitutional court has nothing to do with it, but the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order of Yugoslavia and other bodies, and the minister spoke of this in public. And I'm not, however, called upon to analyse whether the SSNO and the military leadership actually did the right things based on all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you say that the SSNO asked the Presidency of the SFRY to take additional measures to raise the combat readiness of the JNA but that the Presidency rejected this proposal in spite of numerous problems and attacks on the JNA and the territorial integrity of the federal state. Why and how did the Presidency reject this proposal by the military top leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were bogged down. Tens of thousands of young people from Serbia and probably from other areas too had left the country. The mobilisation was collapsing. Whole units were leaving their positions. The Federal Secretariat was asking for additional mobilisation of I don't know how many thousand conscripts more than had already been called up, and the Presidency evaluated that this additional mobilisation would not solve the problems. That's how it was, more or less. That's why they rejected additional mobilisation. There were some disputes between Mr. Jovic and Mr. Kadijevic about this. They were saying, "Do you need that much? Is this much sufficient? You asked for so many and that's not enough now." But this was between them, and I wouldn't like to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, General, since you spoke here of volunteers --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the reasons you have just stated, were they also the reasons for the issuing of these decrees or other documents on the enlistment of volunteers in order to bring up to manpower levels the army units? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were two orders issued by the Presidency. One, as far as I remember, was in January 1991 on the disbanding of paramilitaries. That is the ZNG. And they even referred to the Territorial Defence of Slovenia. But this second order refers to all paramilitary units, including those from Serbia who were going here and there with or without someone's knowledge. If they wanted to fight for a single state, they would have to enter the single system of armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you agree that this was the only proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the only proper thing to do, but it was probably not fully complied with. Not just probably but certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, while you were active --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt. It's time for the adjournment now. We'll go on to that question afterwards. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, please make your answers as brief as possible because my time is limited. Tell me in brief, what was the position of the staff of the Supreme Command of the JNA toward paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative; they were to be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were orders issued to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the instructions of the government, there was also an order of the Federal Secretary and of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how imprisoned members of the JNA were treated in Bjelovar, Gospic, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how they were treated?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, inhumanely. In Gospic, an officer had his throat cut in front of a line of ten of his soldiers in a barracks. And in Bjelovar, an officer of mine who used to serve under me in the Subotica, he was now the brigade commander in Bjelovar, he was -- his brigade was surrounded by the ZNG members. They couldn't shoot at them from the barracks because there were buildings all around. And they imprisoned the commander and two other officers, stripped them naked, and shot them. I think this illustrates what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, how were families of JNA officers living in Croatia treated?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a slogan that they were Serb Chetniks, that is, the JNA. That's how they treated their families too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since from your statement I can see that you say that the HOS numbered over 250.000 soldiers at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that, but that's not reliable information because it varied between 200 and 300.000 soldiers, as General Kadijevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're both being asked to slow down for the interpreters. You speak the same language, there is a temptation to go too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, how many members of the JNA were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think it was between 12 and 15.000 members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was the role of the JNA at the time, or to be more precise, is it correct that on the basis of the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY the only role of the JNA was to create a buffer zone between the paramilitary formations of Croatia and the self-organised Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the circumstances you are aware of, is it true that in Croatia the JNA was forced to defend itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have mentioned this in my written statement. They were to comply with the rules of the service. The commanders were obliged to use the combat rules if they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they forced to apply these rules because they were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, they had to defend themselves only when it was necessary to -- to implement self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any operations on the territory of Serbia by the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four. Sid between Ilok and Backa Palanka, around the bridge in Backa Palanka, then in Apatin, and there was a terrorist group that crossed the Danube in armoured personnel carriers. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what sort of attacks were these? What sort of units and weapons were used?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything from rifles -- from rifles to 350 or 55 millimetre guns near Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the response of the JNA and the government of Serbia to these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia then decided to mobilise the Territorial Defence from several municipalities, and there were political protests, and I don't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, did the JNA want some sort of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had the JNA wanted war, I would have taken off my uniform. I would not have left in the regular way that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Presidency of the SFRY under these circumstances on the 3rd of October declared that there was an imminent threat of war, in accordance with the constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the imminent threat of war consist of?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potential threats of armed attack on part of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina. But may I add in connection with that decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the Presidency, composed of six members out of eight -- six were present; the Slovenian representative, Dr. Drnovsek, and the president of Croatia, Mr. Mesic, were absent. So the Serbian four, conditionally speaking, were there from Serbia, Vojvodina, Kosovo and Metohija, and Montenegro. There was also Bogic Bogicevic of Bosnia and Vasil Tupurkovski, Dr. Vasil Tupurkovski of Macedonia. This decision was reached on that occasion, but as far as I know, the last two, from Bosnia and Macedonia, almost never turned up at meetings of the Presidency any more. And this was - I have to say what my opinion is - a manoeuvre to evade the Presidency rules of procedure which says that if five out of eight members vote in favour of a certain decision, then the decision is valid. The six who were present declared an imminent threat of war, and in this way the Presidency was transformed into the Supreme Command. The Supreme Command does not have the same rules of procedure, so the same number of members is not required to be present. We, the generals and the citizens, have no idea how many members of the Presidency were meeting when something was announced, when a communique was issued, whether they were meeting as the Supreme Command or whether all of them were present. So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, when this decision was reached, six members were present?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So this decision was issued legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, is it true that the Presidency of the SFRY requested that UN peacekeeping forces and European Union monitors come to the territory of the SFRY? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether the Supreme Command of the JNA had direct command over the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here and there perhaps the General Staff would address the TO staff of Krajina if there was a break in communications. But the command of the military district was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, did it carry out its tasks in accordance with the constitution of the SFRY and the constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I stated that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one point, General, because when on page 16 you quote the constitution --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an error. Paragraph 3, 9, 119. That's a mistake. I tried to correct that later on. But the numbers are wrong, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, I don't wish to refer to your statement too often. You mentioned the competencies from the constitution of Serbia, and you failed to mention a particular article. And I don't take it against you, because it does not cover competencies, but it does have great significance because Article 135, paragraph 1, says: "The rights and duties which the Republic of Serbia, which is within the SFRY and which it has according to this constitution and which according to the federal constitution are implemented in the federation, will be implemented in accordance with the federal constitution."

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let us now move on to what you said yesterday about your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Coordination Group. As a Coordination Group, your task was to collect information about the situation in Krajina on the basis of, let us be specific, a task received, an assignment received from the Secretariat for National Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should be, but I cannot assert that because I wasn't present when such a decision was taken. Not by the Republic of Serbia but the Federal Secretariat. So as to ease the burden on the commands, the ministry was given this task to coordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this group worked for the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, a part of the -- its duties which were increasing and which, in a sense, meant assisting the bodies of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and partly also for the Republic of Serbia, which is quite normal as it was a body of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Ministry of Defence of Serbia did not take part in any operative planning?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my statement, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying it. The ministry assisted within the tasks of the SSNO. That is the Federal Secretariat. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the ministry did not -- was not engaged in the training of forces of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only that one case I mentioned when Captain Dragan came, and nothing came of it. I know of no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And so this group was an ad hoc group, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were assigned to that group by the personnel administration of the Federal Secretariat, the SSNO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I gathered from your live testimony here and the explanations you gave, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that you had already handed in your request for retirement, but in view of the situation, you felt that it would not be right for you to retire because you could still be of assistance. Were those your motives for asking your retirement to be postponed, to be able to assist in the newly created situation which was extremely grave? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was your only motive?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basic motive. No other ambitions. And the direct cause was the killing of an officer, my colonel, that I attended his funeral, and this was the last drop that prompted me to take that decision. I had no ambitions of acquiring any orders or any honours or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, your coordination group consisted of some 10 officers. You've said seven to ten. They were either retired or about to be retired.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had already received a decree on retirement on the 31st of December or had already retired. So they were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their professional knowledge was being used in order to assist in gathering information, reviewing the situation and briefing the appropriate bodies of the SSNO about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, in addition to its regular inspection service, the main inspection of National Defence, can also form separate professional bodies and teams for particular professional duties to assist the lower-level communities, and on those grounds, pursuant to the law on national defence, we as the professional body of the ministry were formed to establish contacts and address those problems to relieve the burden on the Federal Secretariat, the district commands, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it right that Simovic informed me about the formation of that Coordination Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that he told you or briefed you about it. He simply informed you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He informed me that such a group had been formed?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with instructions from the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said to you, but I do know that he informed you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that if he informed me, he also told me that something had been formed and not that a body of Serbia had formed such a group.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He informed you that a Coordination Group had been formed. Now, what the explanation was that he gave you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You listed several tasks that you had as a coordinating group. You said to implement requests for replenishment with officers, material assistance, assistance regarding the TO structure, and preparation of or, rather, their education and training to accept the UN forces, and also the question of salaries. Finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I included that under "material assistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that group have any other tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. Tasks cropped up as unannounced people came from Krajina raising various problems, from personal problems to various others. A representative of the municipality or of the TO. And then Minister Simovic would draw the attention of the TO command in Krajina that all those requests and needs should be put in some sort of order and united, pulled together so that individuals would not come with those requests but that it should go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with the meeting of these requests for officers, what was your role except to forward those requests to the personnel administration of the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
