utterances.text: Either forwarding those requests in written form or I and my officers went there in person, or the head of the personnel administration would come to see us and we would arrange things together. Also, with the command of the military district, we inquired about people who were available, and we were a kind of link in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can we infer that in view of the large number of requests and the large number of people coming to seek assistance, a great deal of pressure, some unrealistic demands, you were a kind of filter. You carried out a certain triage of all these requests.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we were able. If we had had greater authority, maybe we would have done a better job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When talking about material assistance, is it true that all the logistics were the responsibility of the competent JNA commands in the particular zones?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but there is a distinction that should be made. Food, medical supplies, things that are not, strictly speaking, military equipment. This was distributed among the municipalities. Manoeuvre structures, that is brigades of the Territorial Defence, relied logistically on the corps commands, the JNA commands of operative groups and their logistic bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that in its entirety in accordance with the forces -- with the rules in force about the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Milosevic, that according to the law on national defence of SFRY and, maybe this is something I didn't mention, the law on the manufacture of weapons and military equipment and the distribution of the same, Article 60. The Federal Secretariat for National Defence has the exclusive competence in that area. This may be something that is difficult to understand. Every republic pays for the weapons, but it doesn't have the right to decide how many weapons it will purchase for a particular factory. Those funds are distributed by the Federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this logistic reliance, as the whole of Yugoslavia was divided into three military districts at the time -- yes, districts --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, four. But the fourth was annulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, the military naval one.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; Zagreb, Sarajevo, Belgrade and Skopje. But the Skopje military district for the ground forces was abolished, so three remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they relied on the logistic bases of those military districts.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, that was how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And according to your knowledge - I've taken this down, I just wanted to check the figure - in connection with these requests for officers, there were 20 to 30 officers sent to the staff of the TO in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to the best of my recollection, but I'm not claiming that. Maybe a few more, but it would be easy to check from the documents that Mr. Nice has presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was within the competence of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system was as follows: When we agreed on the number of personnel, the personnel administration would assign the officers to the TO staff, sometimes specifying to a particular brigade or a particular headquarters. As for the other officers with their names and surnames, the Krajina command of the Territorial Defence would assign to particular positions in the establishment. There was a combination of both systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some documents were produced here relating financial assistance, monetary assistance. Was it provided in accordance with the laws in force?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. According to the law on national defence of the SFRY, the officer or commander who gives assignments to subordinate commands, if the planned funds which have been earmarked in advance for subordinate commands are insufficient, the difference up to the necessary amount is covered by the person issuing the assignment. So that is quite clear. Now, why I said also no: Because each republic, out of its own Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. resources, finances the Territorial Defence, including weapons, without the part it earmarks for the federal budget and the JNA. So it is twofold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is that both is in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, was the relationship between the Defence Ministry and the TO of Krajina a relationship of issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. They gave advice, transferred guidelines, setting requirements but not as a superior but simply for us to analyse those requests and forward them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you had no right of decision-making. The right of decision-making was with the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In the field, some people demanded that a division of the Territorial Defence be formed, or a partisan division. But Milan Babic wouldn't hear of it because it reminded him of the partisans of the five-cornered stars and so on. He wanted something of his own. And then they consulted with us, and we told them, "You can do as follows: You have this option which has such consequences, this option has such-and-such consequences." But we didn't decide. It was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So actually, your role was that of some sort of professional consultant.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that we were a professional body attached to the Ministry of Defence along the line of the SSNO and the ministry of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let us make that quite clear. You could not have any authority, or rather, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia had no authority to decide on the use of units of the TO of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor with respect to the selection of personnel. The Minister of Defence of the TO of Krajina, a certain Tarbuk or something like that, I can't remember, had already been appointed by the government of Krajina. And as far as we knew, he was undesirable. He was not a suitable person for that position. Milan Babic insisted on him retaining that position. However, neither Minister Simovic and myself still less had any authority to order him to replace him because this had to go through the Assembly and through the authorities. Whom they elected later on I don't know, but this is an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that anyone else apart from Milan Babic having that type of intervention for personnel selection? Was anyone bringing pressure to bear on you for someone to be appointed or replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember regarding Mr. Hadzic. He may have intervened for one or two officers, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it now quite clear that the Coordination Group of the Ministry of Defence that you headed, and the Ministry of Defence of Serbia as a whole, could not have anything to do with deployment or operations in the territory of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said in my statement. There were some disputes between the corps commands. Some wanted to have a brigade under his command, and the TO wanted it under their command, but they had to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 19, in paragraph 1, you said that you would occasionally receive information about illegal activities of certain Serbian paramilitary groups. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have testified about that. I think there's no point in repeating that. I spoke about that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the ministry require proceedings to be instituted against such groups?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that General Simovic made a very sharp warning to President Babic and the commander of the TO of Krajina that such cases, should they arise, had to be processed. All the municipalities had courts to do this. It had to go through the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us make this quite clear: The ministry of Serbia could not have competence over them, but it did energetically issue warnings and insist and request that such illegal activities be halted and the perpetrators punished. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. And in a report to the General Staff, among other issues, we referred to that too in written form. And then came the orders on disbanding, on preventing parties to form units and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that such cases were mostly in August and September 1991. Later they were reduced in scope. What contributed to that reduction of undesired incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of Vukovar, Slunj as towns and a little around Okucani, the rest was stabilised, the front was stabilised. The situation had stabilised. Authorities had been formed. The ZNGs did not enter these areas except where there was fighting in these three locations. There may have been some incursions elsewhere but I didn't have detailed information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these measures contribute to the scope of those illegal activities to be reduced.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the overall situation contributed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the ministry, since you also mention the relationship between the minister and the ministry with me as the president of Serbia, was it based exclusively on limits required by the law?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that I, as the president of the republic, at any time did I ask the ministry to implement any decision within the competency of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this period. Only when you had discussions on the law on national defence or the army of Serbia. I don't know what the exact wording was. I know that you postponed further work on this, but I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards legislation, it is the government that tables bills, and the text is prepared by the competent ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the Assembly adopts legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly debates and adopts legislation. So the enactment of legislation or, rather, the preparation for the enactment of legislation is within the competency of the ministry; is that correct? You say that I met General Simovic on only three occasions while you were holding your office.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be quite sure, but as far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many months did you work in that group?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean -- that means I met him a little more than once a month. Does that seem logical to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it's logical, but I think there's no point in discussing this. It's a question of leadership style. It might be more logical to meet more often. I know while I was the Secretary for National Defence during peacetime, there was hardly a month when I did not visit either the Presidency or the Council for the Constitutional Order or some other body, so I don't think that's important now. Two or three times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that I didn't care about the Ministry of Defence very often because I didn't esteem Simovic enough; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my personal opinion. I assume because soon after his appointment General Simovic was transferred from that duty and this was at a crucial point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that I didn't esteem General Simovic enough?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, because you allowed him to be moved to a less important duty, a less significant one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, when the appointment of generals is at stake, it's the SSNO that -- whose opinion is asked.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we pass over this question, for your sake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Why? Can you give us the answer to the question? The question is, and perhaps you can help us with the answer, help the Trial Chamber, General, with the answer: When the appointment of generals is at stake, it's the SSNO whose opinion is asked. Now, can you give us the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, formally that is so, but in reality it's not like that. Mr. Milosevic required his generals to tell him what generals could be counted on and which ones couldn't be counted on. I don't know what the exact formulation was. He'd say, "Let's discuss the generals who are still in the JNA." At that meeting at Mr. Milosevic's, while I was the Secretary for National Defence, Mr. Bogdanovic, an associate of mine, was sitting there with his notebook when these two generals came in. The Ministry of Defence of Serbia reminded Mr. Milosevic by saying, "Mr. President, I cannot give you an objective assessment because these are comrades of mine. I might be wrong in either a positive or a negative way if you ask me about any of them. I suggest that you talk to the SSNO, to the personnel administration. They know which general served where, what his assessment was, his character, his characteristics, and then you will get an objective picture." The same moment, Mr. Milosevic interrupted the conversation and said, "Oh, let's have a whisky. We won't talk about this any more." Thank you for asking me this, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome. I'm happy to oblige. But this has nothing to do with the appointment or dismissal of Simovic, nor does it explain this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question. Tell me, please, was the relationship between me and Simovic, the Minister of Defence, an official, professional one in view of the offices we held at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But the conversation I have just described shows how much you trusted him, whether he was your man or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what "my man" means.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means obedient to you in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I never considered -- I always thought that everybody was his own man, and if he wasn't, he couldn't do anything worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Simovic was his own man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, did it have any role to play or any influence on the events? We've already discussed Croatia, but any influence on the events in Slovenia or Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had nothing to do with Slovenia at the time, either physically or in organisational terms. As regards Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had no contacts in connection with any issues concerning arming or preparations or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is it beyond doubt then that all these events and everything that was done at the time fell within the competency of the federal organs, the Presidency of the SFRY, the General Staff, and the Secretariat for National Defence as the highest civilian and military authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this explain my infrequent contacts with Simovic? There was a vertical chain of command, and as you know, the republican officials, including the presidents of the republics, had no competency there. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, but it doesn't explain what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that's how it is. Whether it explains my question, that's another matter. Please, let me just look, since your statement is quite voluminous. I've made a note here.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's voluminous where we speak of the causes of war. The rest is relatively brief and concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, on page 20, paragraph 3 -- I want you to clarify this. In connection with these issues, it even refers to the Territorial Defence of each republic, including Serbia. You say -- I'll read the whole paragraph: "The Territorial Defence was directly subordinated to the republics. At lower levels, such as zones, regions or municipalities, it was subordinate to the local presidents of municipalities. One should bear in mind that although the TO was subordinate to the presidents of the republics, they did not -- they did not, I repeat, issue direct decisions as to the deployment of the TO. The commander of the TO would do this, and he was subordinate to the staff of the Supreme Command (the SSNO and the General Staff)." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but I wish to introduce a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are my question [as interpreted], but it's not deployment, it's use. The use, not the deployment of TO units. So the issuing of wartime assignments, not simple deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even better. Thank you for this clarification. So the Territorial Defence was fully integrated or, as you soldiers will say, completely networked into the chain of command. And there was singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If part of the territory was on temporarily occupied territory, that is cut off by enemy units, then there was an exception. Then the -- the authorities in that part of the territory would command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the authorities, the local authorities on the occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "occupied" is not the right word. It wasn't recognised in the constitution, but it was a temporarily captured territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have already discussed this, so I won't quote. You say the minister had no competence to punish any group, and he would apply to the competent --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some repetitions here because there were two investigators and when I was nearing the end of my statement, the second investigator, who wasn't fully informed of what the first one had asked, would ask me some questions again. But it doesn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in connection with what you say in your statement on page 23, you say that some political parties started criticising the JNA. They started establishing their own paramilitary units and sending them off to Serbian areas in Croatia where they were at first welcomed by the local TO. Later, this changed when they started looting and killing.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me emphasise. This is in the past in relation to my office. I am not speaking of the second half of November, the second half of December. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about the time here. But it says that paramilitary units -- General, I want to establish here the fact that it was not the leadership of the Krajina that could be held responsible for a paramilitary formation somewhere on the ground in the maelstrom of war. Do you know that they tried to drive them out of there because various groups were roaming around, looting and murdering? They were not people who had come to really assist in defence. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's exactly how it was, but I have no reliable information. I know that there was cooperation. I don't know whether they were expelled. I don't remember anything like that, but I can't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had hoped you would be able to say more about this because here we keep coming across attempts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can say no more, so there's no need to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this point now. It is not clear to me, General, your explanation, that is, about Radmilo Bogdanovic. I understood you to say that Radmilo Bogdanovic, when he was no longer a minister, continued in a way to perform this office indirectly. From what you said, that's what I conclude, and I want to have this clarified because this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. He was a kind of shadow minister. He was an advisor -- not a shadow minister, he was an advisor. He didn't command the police of Serbia at that time, no way. But as Zoran Sokolovic was simply not a man who was up to the job, he had no experience, it was natural for Radmilo Bogdanovic to go there so that they could consult and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. You used a rather strong term when you say that Zoran Sokolovic was not up to the job.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to insult him but this was not his profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Profession is one thing but function of minister is a political office.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware of the fact that Zoran Sokolovic held a much higher office than Radmilo Bogdanovic and that in no way could Radmilo Bogdanovic have controlled Zoran Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he controlled him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Sokolovic, if you remember, was the secretary of the Central Committee at the time when Bogdanovic was the Assistant Minister of Defence at the republic level, which means a secondary level. And later on, he was the speaker of parliament. So in no way could Radmilo Bogdanovic have had authority over him.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Zoran Sokolovic is dead. Let's not insult the deceased. I have been quite clear. Please let's not go into this. Authority. Of course he was an authority for Zoran. Radmilo was in the SUP regional community, he was a minister in three or four or five terms, the Minister of Defence; he knew the territory, he knew the people, he knew the circumstances, he knew the security situation in Serbia. Zoran dealt more with party work. That's what I meant to say. If you're looking for something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify this one point. After he ceased to be Minister of the Interior, he was no longer able to carry out this job either directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not through Zoran Sokolovic with whom he was not in a close relationship.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's discuss some other matters, General. You made some corrections to your statement, and you say paragraph 24. I don't know where it is but that's what it says here. The Federal Secretariat for National Defence asked the Presidency of the SFRY to have the republics of Serbia and Montenegro undertake to provide material support for the armed forces. Why did you introduce this correction?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the original text, it appeared that the Presidency was asking this, but it was actually the general -- it was actually General Kadijevic asking this of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of the Presidency. Not of Serbia and Montenegro but of the Presidency that Serbia and Montenegro should fulfil their --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, their material obligations to fund the JNA, because the other republics had stopped investing in the budget, had stopped putting money into the budget. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the budget now. You said that the budget, the federal budget, was spent mostly on the army and the republican budget mostly on the police. General, would you allow that you do not know this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The army is federal, and 90 per cent of the federal budget was spent on the army -- 70 per cent. And the republican budget, of any republic, had to finance health care, education, public services, interventions in the economy, and so on and so forth. Can you say that you do not know that most of the budget and that the share of the expenses of the army in the federal budget cannot be compared with the share of the police in the republican budget?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's not weary the Chamber or the public. I do not have precise information, figures, at my disposal. But if you're talking about health care, it was a very small fraction, or other forms of expenses. Most of the funds were spent on the police, just as in the federal budget most of the funds were spent on the army. But there was a disproportion between the Serbian budget and the Yugoslav budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you discussed at the meeting of retired generals with Perisic. I just wanted to establish whether you know this at all. And it's not hard to find the appropriate figures.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not even necessary to establish them. You said that I paid more attention to the police than the army. But I was the president of the Republic of Serbia, therefore I could not have any competency over the army, and certainly I did care about the police as it was the police of the Republic of Serbia. So what's strange there if I take care of what is my duty to do and don't take care about things that it is not my job?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as a citizen of Yugoslavia, I feel ashamed to say to you that the police, for the past I don't know how many years, shall we say from the time when you came to power was better equipped materially, better taken care of than members of the army of Yugoslavia. Even today the situation, unfortunately, is not much better. Those are facts. And don't fatigue me now with the figures, whether it's this much or that much, when the entire public in Yugoslavia is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know these things. I just asked you in view of your allegation that I concern myself with the police and not with the army. Serbia did not have an army for me to take care of them. I took care of the army when I became president of Yugoslavia and when that was my duty. Is that right or not, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but Serbia was preparing the police to be transformed into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. Do you have any evidence to corroborate this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quantity of weapons given by the army to the police is not necessary under normal conditions. That is one of the parameters. Another is financing. And I don't want to enumerate because of the shame I feel of all that was done and what the army suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that no one in Serbia, at least when the authorities are in question, had a negative attitude to the army.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no, but I'm talking about the funding, as a result of which our soldiers had dry food three times a day, no heating, no uniforms, they couldn't keep the equipment in good repair and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. One at a time, and remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the other day I quoted here when I was accused of giving instructions to finance and provide funds outside the budget to finance the army of Yugoslavia, and then I asked, So what if I assisted the army of my state, of my country? How can you then say now that I had a negative attitude to the army, for heaven's sake?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was negative by the Serb people or by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you testify against me here and you're saying my attitude towards the army. Do you believe that I had a negative attitude towards the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me say first of all that I have not come to testify against you. I have been invited and the federal government on the 3rd of March gave me permission to appear here to testify about the things I took part in and what I know from that period. Whether this will be relevant for the Court against you or in favour of you, I don't know that. So please don't make me say that you hated the army. You did not. But you did not respect it in -- to the extent to which you could have to assist the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that I didn't assist it as far as I was able? How do you know that? How did you know that I didn't assist as far as I could? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as much as you could but as much as was needed as compared to the funds earmarked for some other purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us not allow this to be transformed into a political debate. Let Mr. Milosevic put specific questions to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will make sure it's not a political debate, but this question about support for the police or support for the army may be an important one which we have to consider. So if the accused has any more questions about it, then he's entitled to ask them. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got half an hour left, if you want it. You don't have to use it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that that is the customary position taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have been shown here many exhibits concerning finances. I was unable to register all of them, nor do I consider it important, but for instance, they asked you to comment on Martic's letter to Zoran Sokolovic to the effect that certain funds from the SDK in Glina be transferred to the Ministry of the Interior which, as he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just identify it. Tab 11, let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecution 406.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you need anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, so what if the Minister of Defence of Krajina writes to the Minister of Defence of Serbia, therefore his colleague, and appeals to him to intervene for certain funds which are already there to be transferred? What's a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior to the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I made a slip of the tongue. The Minister of the Interior of Krajina, the Minister of Interior of Serbia. So these are Ministers of Internal Affairs. When the minister of Krajina appeals to his colleague the minister in Serbia to intervene so that these funds be transferred to them which are on a particular account. Do you, in view of your knowledge, experience, and the facts at your disposal from those times, see anything in law -- illegal, suspicious, or criminal in that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that was not raised at all by me, nor did I hear a question to that effect being put to me. Then I was asked whether this document is authentic, but let me explain. The Minister of Internal Affairs of Krajina, Mr. Milan Martic, asks for funds, financial funds, resources, which had already been allocated to the Territorial Defence in the social accounting service of Glina SDK and which had not been used, which had not been spent. And he's asking Minister Sokolovic for these funds to be transferred to him. I don't see that there's anything unjustified in this request. I was just asked whether this can be linked to the financing of the Territorial Defence. I apologise, Mr. Nice [sic], maybe you can repeat your question. I don't know what is in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the police of Krajina, was it then acting in defence of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're asking me something that is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since it's obvious, that's why I'm asking. Isn't all this logical?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't criticise this document. I don't know why you're asking me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am glad to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just commented on it, saying that these were funds which had already been earmarked by Belgrade for Krajina. They were on an account in Glina. They had not been spent. Martic knew about it, and he asked for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please look at tab 15. General, I put a question to you about the treatment for captured prisoners or, rather, officers and soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone has been switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you put your microphone on again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when I asked you the question about the treatment of captured soldiers and officers of the JNA in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you answered, if I remember well, I didn't note it down, that they were treated inhumanely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have here an order of the Chief of Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY under the heading "Strict observation of international humanitarian law." Would you be kind enough, General, to comment on this order. The best idea would be for you to read out what you consider to be essential from that order, to read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, the most important is paragraph 4, or point 4. "All breaches of the regulations of international humanitarian law," et cetera, "should be reported with documentation to proper legal military organs who will take adequate action as envisaged by the law against the perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I thought it was not necessary to read it all out.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do I think number 4 to be the most important? Because all the rest under number 1, 2, 3 and 5 can be considered as something that was already well known to the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, because at the military academy, the staff academy, especially the School of National Defence, they had separate subjects, topics in strategy and tactics under the heading "Procedure and care of prisoners of war." That was the heading in short. But those lectures were based on the regulations signed or proclaimed by decree by the president of the Presidency of SFRY - I think it was Lazar Mojsov - in 1988. I'm not wrong about the date. I'm not sure if he was still the president of the Presidency at the time. And in accordance with that decree, the Federal Secretary of National Defence issued regulations about the implementation of international humanitarian war law, the Geneva Conventions, The Hague Conventions, the Customs of War, and all these relevant documents are enumerated. In other words, the Chief of Staff by this order is reminding of the officers of something that they should have known and gives them order that what is written in those regulations should be implemented to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what is important here is the date, the 14th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the time when, for several months if not for a whole year by then, General, there were various horrific crimes being committed against members of the JNA, bestial crimes, and also against Serb civilians in Croatia, and the order is being given by reminding of all those provisions that each breach - each; there is the word each and every here, or all: "All breaches ... in the area of the unit's activities must be reported and documentation available submitted to proper legal military organs who will take adequate action against the perpetrators as stipulated by law." I'm asking you now, General, whether the JNA as a whole complied with these obligations and the stipulations of this order regarding humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did, but I cannot assert that there were individual excesses or deviations in relation to the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, there may always be individual excesses. I'm not asking you about them. I'm asking you, as you were active at the time, you were a general and you know this, whether the JNA, the armed forces abided by these rules prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, at the end of today's examination-in-chief, you were answering questions from Mr. Nice, and one of the last questions by my learned friend had to do with the attack of the air force on the capital of Slovenia, which never took place. I would like to ask you to answer a number of questions so that we might assist Their Honours to understand that situation, and that is why I will have to read out a very short paragraph from the statement you gave to the investigators before I put any question to you. In that statement, you said the following: "The unconstitutional formation of paramilitary forces that were called the ZNGs by members of the party that was in power, the HDZ, the illegal and unlawful import of weapons in 1991 in Croatia, there were already 60.000 members of the ZNG under arms and about 7.000 armed policemen. In Slovenia, close to Maribor, there was an inspection group consisting of 30.000 members of the Slovenian army, which was a paramilitary formation outside the structure of the armed forces of the SFRY in 1990. Those armed forces were prepared to be ready to violate the constitutional order of the SFRY. General plans were devised for these formations to attack JNA units on the territory of Croatia." A moment ago, in answer to a question by Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, you told us what happened, but you also said here that already then plans were being made for liquidation of JNA officers and other plans linked to the attacks on the JNA. Is what you stated then correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only maybe it's not written quite correctly. When I talked about an inspection group, it would be better to say that there was a review of members of about 30.000 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And these were all armed members of the Slovenian army?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we come to my question, the first question I would like to put to you in that connection. You spoke about Mr. Jovic's book, Borisav Jovic's book, not Slobodan, I'm sorry. But you also are familiar with Veljko Kadijevic's book and you've read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have only one question in that connection. Did the Supreme Command know, as is written in this book, that there were plans outside, abroad, and also inside the country either to provoke the army to act first in a certain way and to then respond with these paramilitary units, or to actually directly attack the JNA first if the first option is not successful? General Kadijevic writes about that in the first part of the book. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government of Yugoslavia, headed by Ante Markovic -- this is also contained in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- had decided to retake the border so as to prevent incursions in the first place of armed units from abroad, from outside the country.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that point was overemphasised. It should read as follows: "The federal Executive Council and its president, Ante Markovic, took a decision to establish the customs regime, the functioning of payment transactions, and to provide customs duty in accordance with the federal laws." However, as there was information that certain small groups may break in from Italy or Austria to assist them, not to carry out aggression but simply to make it known that they had friends in those countries, it was decided that the JNA should re-establish its control over the border posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. That's what it says. But you go on to say that the federal government took a decision and through the SSNO, 1.990 soldiers were sent to retake the border posts, the external borders of the country.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The task was carried out, but the newly formed Slovenian armed units, numbering about 35 to 40.000 men, attacked small military columns and groups and border posts - these were posts on the border with Austria and Italy - and 43 JNA soldiers were killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is: The attack that was prepared by the JNA and was halted, should it have happened after all this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the air raid? Yes, it should have taken place if these incidents were not halted after the agreement reached in Ljubljana, because there were some more attacks after that date. Mr. Tapuskovic, after the agreement reached in Ljubljana between Mesic, Ante Markovic, Kucan, Stane Brovet, I don't know who else was there on behalf of the JNA, on the immediate cessation of fire for another two or three days, the Slovenian territorial units opened fire in individual cases. And then there was the possibility of attacks not on Ljubljana but transport routes, weapons warehouses, relay stations, which would cause certain losses, material losses, to force a collapse in Slovenia and to force it to abide by the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that did not happen, and after that, Croatia attacked several rail convoys carrying equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's time for the break, but I would have a few more questions to cover with this witness, one other topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now, twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to ask the witness Mr. Djordjevic to explain a few other points to the Chamber in connection with the way the law on national defence of Serbia was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this during the examination-in-chief. I would like to ask you to explain to the Chamber under what circumstances the law on all people's defence was implemented and under what circumstances you were active within the scope of the body you were working in. You may not have it in front of you, but I assume you know it by heart. The Article 1 of the law on all people's defence speaks of the functioning of all people's defence and provides for the circumstances. First, in case of an attack on the country. This was not the case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second provision is if there is imminent threat of war. From the 3rd of October onwards, imminent threat of war was proclaimed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another provision states that if there are emergency situations, this can be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A state of emergency is mentioned that's similar to what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, these are unusual circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigators, you described the circumstances under which you were working even before an imminent threat of war was proclaimed. You mentioned the arrival of refugees from Croatia, including retired military, young men who were of an age to serve in the army, also reservists whose units had been disbanded in Croatia. First, would you tell the Chamber whether at that time, before October 1991, there were refugees and to what extent. Not only retired officers, but how many refugees there were already in Serbia at that time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers, but the numbers grew from month-to-month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the final number was reached after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also say that a large number of wounded arrived, families of people who had been killed, and that help to be given to these people and these families.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you mention the hardships suffered by members of the JNA in the barracks and the inhumane treatment of their families in places where they lived in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just give one more illustration: Deserting from some units and refusal to help the surrounded and imperilled units in Croatia. In other words, everybody wanted to preserve Yugoslavia, but they were only paying lip-service to this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and General Veljko Kadijevic also mentioned this in his book, the Federal Secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what exactly you were referring to when you spoke of the implementation of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. You said there were three main tasks that you were in charge of. This is on page 15 of your statement, where you say: "The first task under the constitution was the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the Republic of Serbia. Second, the defence and security of the Republic of Serbia, and also other relations of interest for the Republic of Serbia." And then you say that the Republic of Serbia maintained connections with Serbs living outside the Republic of Serbia in order to preserve their national and cultural and historical identity.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, I listed three out of 30-odd tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the major ones?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the major ones. For example, I didn't mention developing the plan of defence by the ministry, participation in the plan of defence of the republics, organisation of the leadership of republican organs, coding and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were these the tasks that you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, my question is: Do you know that there was a plan? Do you know of any plan or any decision connected to territorial pretensions that Serbia might have had toward any other republic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for what I read in Boro Jovic's book and also Veljko Kadijevic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But a particular decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In public, in the bodies of government, Greater Serbia was never mentioned, nor did we as officers count on this. What was spoken of was Yugoslavia among us officers, up to the Karavanke alp mountain range. And Boro Jovic, Milosevic - I apologise for pointing with my finger - when they spoke among themselves, they did not mention a Greater Serbia, they spoke of Yugoslavia and those who wanted to live in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody who took part in these events is writing books now. But what I want to know is, did the Assembly of Serbia, the parliament or any other organ of government issue any decisions containing pretensions of Serbia towards the territory of others?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said here that these were megalomaniac requests.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is do you know of any assistance that can be expressed? Do you know how these requests were resolved, how they were answered?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there was a special officer who was in part of the financial aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you know of no documents showing how much money went from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for what I have seen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What have you now learnt from Jovic's book about Greater Serbia that you didn't know before?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if one is to believe the words of Mr. Boro Jovic, in several places in that book, and I have mentioned the page numbers, he states that in conversations between Boro Jovic and Veljko Kadijevic, the two of them alone, tete-a-tete without Mr. Milosevic, they talked about how Slovenia could be driven out of Yugoslavia. This was in June 1990. Because the Slovenes were preparing decisions on independence. In other words, they could not find common ground as to how the SFRY was to be reorganised. And then Boro said, "I would do it, but what do you think?" And Veljko Kadijevic, at that time, wasn't thinking in that way and he was trying to avoid a direct answer. And then Boro added - I'm referring to Dr. Borisav Jovic - he said, "I would also cut off half of Croatia. Not half, but I would leave the Krajinas where the Serb population lives so that that part remains in Yugoslavia and let the others secede." But no clear decision was reached. A few days later, he called Mr. Milosevic. Dr. Jovic is now talking to Mr. Milosevic about the same topic, and he says more or less Slobodan Milosevic - he doesn't say "Slobo," he says Slobodan Milosevic - was very enthusiastic and put forward two ideas. First, cut off Slovenia over night so that it is no longer part of Yugoslavia; and two, he put forward the same idea with the Krajinas that Boro Jovic had, but Mr. Milosevic asked Dr. Jovic, "I don't know how the army will behave. Would they agree to secure those future borders in that case?" That's what they said in June 1991 again, but that is something that I have read in Dr. Jovic's book. I cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours the whole issue of Jovic's book will arise for consideration later. We've had a number of witnesses speaking of its factual accuracy on certain points. The question of Jovic giving evidence will also, of course, in one format or another arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But can you help us with this, General: Forgetting the books for the time being, just yes or no, did you ever hear the phrase "Greater Serbia" used publicly, and if so, just when did you first hear it referred to? That's all I want. Referred to in public.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this was used almost exclusively by Dr. Vojislav Seselj in public, the president of the Serb Democratic Party. I did not hear anyone else use that phrase in public. Their party even had a magazine entitled "Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now some short questions, I hope. Short, probably. The bombing of Ljubljana, as it was translated in an answer to a question from Mr. Tapuskovic, you said that the bombing of Ljubljana, I think, should have happened. Are you saying that in your judgement as a military man it's something that should have happened or are you saying it's something that would have happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say should have happened, I said it might have happened. It had been prepared. But not Ljubljana as a city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I needed to know. It may well be it was a translation technical problem. Breach of humanitarian law by the army and the fact that the document you looked at showed that they were supposed to bring breaches of humanitarian law to the attention of the legal authorities. Were you aware of any trials taking place reflecting breach of humanitarian laws by JNA soldiers or officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any, which doesn't mean that there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not something that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of the JNA's compliance, to your knowledge, with the requirement of humanitarian law. You were out of office at the end of December 1991. Is it to that period that you were referring or to any other period?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that period. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about the significance of a crime of the transfer of funds in the way that you've helped us with. What you've described is money raised in Serbia being spent, from what you've shown from the documents, on forces operating in another country, the republic -- or another republic, the Republic of Croatia. Do you know one way or another anything about the legality of using money in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Territorial Defence of Krajina, or are you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat, sir: Under the law on national defence of the SFRY, the commanding officer, and in this case I'm referring to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to which the Presidency of the SFRY transferred authority to command the armed forces, both the JNA and the TO, the commanding officer assigning tasks to lower-level commands, if the funds already planned for these lower-level commands are not sufficient for the performance of the task, the commanding officer has the duty to secure the necessary funds. That's as concerns the law on national defence viewed from this aspect. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Each of the republics of the former Yugoslavia set aside 0.4 to 0.6 per cent of the GNP to finance its own Territorial Defence; equipment, weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... General. Croatia was independent as from October of 1991, and the document we were looking at was, I think, January 1992. Do you have any comment to make about the legality or otherwise? It may be outside your area of expertise, the legality or otherwise of financing operations in the Krajina as at that date.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal parliament, I don't know when exactly, issued a decision that decisions on the independence of Slovenia and Croatia were not to be recognised. On this basis, the federal council did not view these countries as independent countries. And conversely, Croatia and Slovenia experienced themselves, on the basis of their parliamentary decisions, as legally inaugurated states. They were to be recognised only as of January 1991 and not by every country at the same time. So that simply I am not qualified to assess this. A lawyer might give you a better answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made the comment and the accused was concerned about this, or was challenging you about this, that the police had been converted or was being converted into the praetorian guard and that you were ashamed as a citizen that the police were better equipped and that Serbia was preparing to convert the police into an army or the army. No motive has been suggested to you by the accused for why you should be making this up or not giving an honest account of your perceptions, but help us with this: In those passages of your evidence, were you giving your experience as a citizen, your experience as a soldier? Just what was it in telling us about the development of this praetorian guard?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the meeting of the Presidency, or you were asked about the meeting of the Presidency that declared the imminent threat of war. Do you actually know yourself who was present there? It's been suggested to you there were six people and it was legally properly composed, but do you actually know that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know myself in the sense that I was there or that I received an official report about it, but it was common knowledge who the six members present were, and the decision taken then was a legal one by a majority of Presidency members regardless of the fact that members of the Presidency from Slovenia and Croatia were not present. However, immediately after that, that Presidency did not meet again as six or eight members, but it started acting as a four-member body. And since a state of imminent threat of war had been proclaimed, then it acts, in relation to defence, more as a Supreme Command. And for the Supreme Command, there is no explicit requirement that all eight members of the Presidency have to be present or only three of them for a decision to be taken. And that is why I expressed the suspicion that this might have been a kind of manoeuvre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And on the topic of the Supreme Command, the Supreme Command can only come into effect after a proper declaration of threat of war or imminent threat of war. Would it have been proper or improper to operate through a Supreme Command before such a declaration?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency is transformed in relation to defence matters in three situations; immediate threat of war, emergencies, or a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is very simple: Would it be proper or improper to operate through a Supreme Command before a valid declaration of one of those three states?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just look, lastly, then, at tab 3 once more to deal with a number questions that have been asked of you, but I really have only got one to deal with. The accused has asked you a number of questions suggesting that all decisions were really being made by the SSNO as a republican -- as a federal body. We see from this diagram that your coordination was within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, and indeed you've told us it was at one stage in the building of a ministry in Serbia. If the requests for assistance, money, or officers were properly made, was there any reason why they shouldn't simply have been made directly through to the SSNO's relevant sectors?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's -- there's only a practical reason, because the SSNO was overburdened with the control of command of the armed forces which had been transferred to it by the Presidency, and so we acted as a kind of place for selecting, sifting through those requests and passing them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I follow that, but the Chamber may be interested to have your comment on this: These were requests coming from Serbs outside Serbia. Indeed, they were coming from a place that had now declared its independence. They were channeled through a body that was within Serbia and indeed within the Serbian Ministry of Defence before it goes to the federal bodies for action and approval. Was there significance in the fact that it was Serbian requests coming through this Serbian body in the state of Serbia, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Federal Secretary for National Defence does have the legal possibility to transfer a part of his competencies to professional or other teams to act on his behalf and to carry out specific tasks. That is one thing. Secondly, you said that they were already independent states. At the Brioni conference on the 7th of July of the same year it had been agreed that decisions on independence be postponed by three months, and this meant sometime around the 7th of October. I can't remember all the interventions made by the European Community and other international factors. And at the last meetings at the top political leadership level, there were discussions to calm things down for a while and to wait so that the SSNO, we in the army, did not really treat them then as de facto independent states. So I simply cannot give you an answer along the lines of your expectations perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And two last questions, one very short and one probably even shorter. You spoke of malicious attitudes towards what was in preparation in Slovenia and Macedonia. On whose part were there malicious attitudes? If you can't remember the phrase, I'll simply move on to the last question.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to this separation or secession of individual republics, there was a principal thesis within the Serbian leadership and also in the Presidency of the SFRY. The position was that the Serbs should remain living in a common state, which meant the SFRY, as there are some in all the republics though in small numbers in Slovenia, but in all the others. However, in response to this thesis, I quoted a position upheld by the Chief of Staff on the 4th or 5th of July when he briefed us in the centre of high military schools when he explicitly said that such a position would lead to bloodshed, because all the republics are inhabited by various ethnic groups and such an aim cannot be achieved without battle, and this would be conducive to a bloody conflict, and a political solution needed to be found. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last point is this: At the break when you were in the company of the usher, perhaps misunderstanding the learned Judge's directions, you looked as though you wanted to either show me something or speak to me and I said no, we couldn't speak. Was there some point of the evidence that you were concerned that you wanted to amplify at that stage? And if so, if you tell us what the topic is and I'll see if there's any further I would like you to answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. For the Court, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to the next topic which may be Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's discussion about 92 bis, can I mention two or three very short administrative things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if it would be convenient to hear the witness first and then deal with administrative matters later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Mine will be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have arranged things to do this afternoon as well. They're just these: Mr. Marinovic is, as you know, on videolink next Monday. There are a number of exhibits. I'm having them produced, including one very large map. I'll have them prepared in advance so that if the Chamber wants to do any pre-reading, including of the large map, it will be available on Friday, and we've made arrangements that there can be both a large map and an overhead projector where his video conference camera will be, matching what we have here. So I hope that one way or another his evidence will be able to be taken quickly but with the best visual aids, and I'll make that arrangement available in advance. And there's one topic that I'd like to mention in closed session for literally two minutes that I didn't touch on in the discussions last week but I invite the Chamber's assistance on. It will literally only take two minutes, if Your Honour would be good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Uertz-Retzlaff, we'll go on until quarter to two with the witness. We'll then spend five minutes on the administrative matters after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Zana Baca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: I'm an art historian and an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the relevant period, did you work at the Institute for Protection of Cultural and Historic Monuments for Dubrovnik; and if so, in what function?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: I did, in the conservation department in Dubrovnik, as an associate art historian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you are, meanwhile, the director of that same institute; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the ICTY on the 27th of June and 19 December 2000. Did you review this statement while you were here and confirm it in a legal proceeding last week?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you make a small addendum on a minor point?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a correction. Instead of "midnight," it should have been "noon."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender the 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let it have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 407.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness gave the statement, she provided a huge amount of documentation, but for practical reasons we deal with the documentation here. We did not combine it with the 92 bis statement. It was for practical reason only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness -- Ms. Baca, when did Dubrovnik become a world heritage site?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: In 1979 Dubrovnik was included in the list of world heritage sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was the old town protected in its entirety, including the walls?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The whole town within the walls and the walls themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you -- are you aware of the nomination documentation that dealt with this issue? Did you discuss the documents, that is, the request to have this -- to have Dubrovnik be included in the world heritage site list?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this regard, the Prosecution would like to tender four documents, and these are actually tabs 6, 7, 8, and 9 in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are the UNESCO documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: UNESCO documents. It's actually a huge amount of documents altogether, and tabbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the exhibit number first for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the five binders will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And actually, I don't think we need to put it to the witness. The witness has actually reviewed the documents. Tab 6 is the documentation, the cover page of the documentation. Tab 7 is the convention concerning the protection of the world cultural heritage, the heritage list actually describing Dubrovnik and how it is included in the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just in relation to that, Ms. Baca, the justification for inclusion of Dubrovnik in the world heritage list is described under paragraph 5 and refers to the complex of Dubrovnik as it has retained over the hundreds of years. And also on that same topic it says in the report, "emphasis is laid upon the importance of the fortified walls." Does that mean Dubrovnik was included because of its unique layout?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: It was included on the UNESCO heritage list not only because of its appearance but because of its urban matrix which was observed from the early Middle Ages, confirmed by the statute from the beginning and end of the thirteenth century, the provisions of which determined the exact method of construction of the town, the width and length of streets, the size of buildings, the method of construction, and everything else of relevance for the existence of a town of that kind. And also, there were provisions regarding its expansion.
