And this urban matrix, this method of construction was retained up to the present day despite the fact that Dubrovnik, in the seventeenth century, suffered a serious earthquake, in 1667, to be precise, and despite of the damage inflicted, through provisions of the Dubrovnik statute, Dubrovnik was renovated pursuant to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the same medieval matrix, which was fully observed, and the same provisions covered the walls. The Golden Age of Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you could tell me: Paragraph 5 of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 of tab 7, and it's page 7 of this document. You find the justification of why this town is included in the list. And tab 8 is actually the original request to have it included. And tab 9 is also related to that same process, the justification on why it is to be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like now to go to the UNESCO Convention. Are you familiar with the UNESCO Convention from 1972?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is tab 3 of that binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to this document, my question is, this Convention, does it in particular refer to obligations of the state in which the protected property is situated?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All the basic provisions of that Convention were complied with except the law on the protection of cultural goods, which is in charge of the preservation of cultural values throughout Croatia. There are also special laws relating to Dubrovnik. In addition to the conservation department in Dubrovnik itself, there is the Institute for the Reconstruction of Dubrovnik, attached to which there is a professional and advisory commission which actually monitors the reconstruction work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we wouldn't need to know all the details. Just the Convention, the UNESCO Convention, as I call it for short reference, is not actually an additional convention in relation to armed conflicts. It's more related to the state, what a state has to do with its property, cultural properties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: The most important thing is to preserve cultural heritage, to cultivate and care for it constantly in accordance with the methodology of the profession, to seek to revitalise buildings, to bring them back to life, to preserve Dubrovnik as a live city, and as much as possible to preserve it with traditional materials, traditional methods, all in accordance with the methodology of the profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in going further with the UNESCO documents, are you familiar with the list, the world heritage list?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The heritage lists confirming actually that the old city of Dubrovnik is included. Are you familiar with this list?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: I know that a list exists. I know that Dubrovnik is included in the list, but of course I couldn't tell you by heart all the towns on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And there is another document that concludes it actually, tab 13, establishment of the world heritage list. In this document, there are actually the criteria for the inclusion of cultural property in this list and the proceeding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is the old town of Dubrovnik also protected by the 1954 Hague Convention for the protection of cultural property in the event of an armed conflict? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, it is protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's tab 2 of the -- of Exhibit 408.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just would like to ask you one question in relation to this. Article 4, respect for cultural property, is actually referring to both sides of a conflict, regarding protection, and it says that the high contracting parties, by refraining from any use of the one party by refraining from any use of the property and its immediate surroundings or of the appliances in use for its protection for purposes which are likely to expose it to destruction or damage in the event of armed conflict, and the other party by refraining from any acts of hostility directed against such property. And in relation to this, I would like to ask you, are you aware or do you know whether any military facilities or military units or police units were stationed in the old town?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: No. There were no such units stationed in the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you in a position to make such observations? Did you move around in the old town?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: All the time. We moved through the old town all the time, drawing up documentation on the war damage. All my colleagues visited almost every street, almost every house all the time we were there, throughout the time within the historical nucleus of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to The Hague convention, in paragraph 5 -- in chapter 5, rather, there is also described the distinctive emblem that is to be used when flagging such -- such buildings, and it's actually also the sign as such is here, drawn in here. My question is: Did you erect such flags and can you tell us something about the sites of these flags and their visibility?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: We erected such signs all over the area for which our conservation service was charged and in the old town. Whenever we erected such a sign, we took photographs, and this is part our documentation. Of course, The Hague Convention was complied with, and the signs were always put up in the most visible places on the buildings. We did this during August and September 1991. And the sign itself is well known. It is a blue and white shield-shaped sign with a blue triangle and a blue rhomboid shape with two white triangles at the sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how big is it?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: 150 by 120 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you did that in summer. Did you actually get a letter from the Ministry of Education and Culture asking you to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We received a letter from the Ministry of Culture and our director followed the instructions in it. She called on all the associates, all the employees who were on vacation at the time to come back to work, including me, and we set about putting up these signs and also protecting movable cultural values within the old town and also in the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's tab 1 of the binder, this letter dealing -- this letter from the 22nd of August, 1991, asking -- asking for protecting the cultural monuments in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And finally, one question in relation to the protection: Are you aware whether the SFRY ratified both Conventions, that is the UNESCO Convention of 1992 and the Hague Convention? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. This is noted in our literature, or rather, it was part of the exam I had to take at the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have also included in the exhibit binder tab 4, that's the ratification of The Hague Convention in January 1956; and tab 5, that is the ratification of the Cultural Heritage Convention, February 1975.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, we do not have to speak about the attack as such. That was done by other witnesses. I only want to speak with you about your damage assessment after the various bombings and shellings, and first of all, after the shelling of the old town in October, did your institute make a damage assessment and prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes. Our institute prepared a report on the damage, and the report was sent to the Ministry of Culture.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this report is tab 17, and I would like to show to the witness just page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You did review this document during your preparation for the testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And here indicated by dots, black dots, are the buildings that were hit, and you have also indicated what the buildings actually are, a synagogue, Sponza Palace. Some are not so visible. "Old Port" it says here, and what are the other words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's see if we can find this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 17, and it's the -- the pages are not numbered, but it's the fifth page when you start from the cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe you can put it on the ELMO, Ms. Baca. Can you put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually both B/C/S and English. Most of all on the same page or the following page, but it's the map just showing the layout of Dubrovnik with the dots in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have indicated here synagogue, Dominican monastery, Sponza Palace, Old Port, but some of the words are not so visible. Can you read the other words? What is it?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: This is the Franciscan monastery, the Bokor fortress, the Rupe museum containing the ethnographical museum and the ethnological museum. This is a residential building, this is the synagogue, the Dominican monastery, as you've already said the Sponza Palace containing the state archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We -- thank you very much. We do not go into the details of the damage found at that time. It's documented in the report. I would like to ask you now about the shelling of the town in mid-November 1991. After this shelling of the old town, did your institute again examine the damage and make a report of this as well?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: That's correct. We did it again. That was our duty, to document, record, make lists and report to the appropriate services. We did make such a list -- rather, report.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's tab 18. That's the report of November 1991, and it's also a combination of B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to show to the witness also the map, the town layout again. It's -- it's the first -- it's the first town map that you see. It's around page 10. And you have here these dots, again the black dots. And what do they indicate? Is that the impacts of shells?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: These are direct hits by shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes. We do not need to go into the --

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Their precise locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That should be enough for these reports, because we have a final huge report that we will come to. Did UNESCO observers arrive in Dubrovnik in November 1991 to monitor the situation and to help your institute assess the damage?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: On the 28th of November until the 20th of December, representatives of UNESCO, Mr. Bruno Carnez and Colin Kaiser stayed in Dubrovnik, and this was the first time the Director General of UNESCO sent a mission to a war-affected area. They were accommodated with us, and they worked in our offices. From that time on we worked together with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them. Our work was joint work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- the letter actually dispatching Colin Kaiser and his colleague is tab 10 in the documentation. The witness was aware of this fact here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on, would that be a convenient time to stop?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, we have to adjourn now. Would you remember during the break not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. And that does include members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back at half past ten tomorrow morning. We have another witness to deal with before then, but we hope to get to your evidence as soon as possible in order to try and conclude it tomorrow. So could you be back, please, at half past ten tomorrow. If you would like to go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, to let you know what I have in mind --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To let you know what we have in mind, on Friday it may be convenient to take an hour or so to try and deal with as many of the applications under Rule 92 bis for the admission of witness statements. And so that everybody can know what to prepare, I have in mind to finish the Vukovar statements which we hadn't finished last week when Judge Kwon and I, you remember, were sitting alone, and we reserved C-1165, C-1164. So we ought to finish those two. Outstanding, I notice, C-1149. There is another Vukovar witness, C-1171, but I think there seems to be an application for his transcript to be admitted. So we will deal with him when we deal with the transcripts. And it might be convenient to deal with all -- any remaining Vukovar and locality witnesses after we've dealt with the application in relation to the transcripts, which we should do next week. We ought to attend to that. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise one matter? And it's matter of convenience. I had a pre-existing commitment from a long while ago to attend something on Friday, and this is an aspect of the evidence that I have dealt with solely. It would be virtually impossible for Mr. Tapuskovic to take it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move it to Thursday. I can't see any great difficulty in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll move it to Thursday. And going on with the matters we should consider, there is an application of the 26th of February for two witnesses, a Mr. Josipovic, C-1156. It may be convenient to deal with them separately. It then would be convenient to make a start, at least, on the Dubrovnik witnesses, and I'm going to list them as I understand it, and we'll note if we've made -- we've made any -- left any out. Apologies to the interpreters. There's a list coming up, but I'm afraid I've only just written out. The list is: C-1066, 1082, 1083, 1088, 1092, 1095, 1105, 1112, 1122, 1127, 1133, 1139, 1150, 1159, 1173. Those are the ones which I've noted as related to Dubrovnik, and it may, as I say, be convenient to deal with them together. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, one matter you may want to consider is whether you really need this amount of witnesses. You might consider pruning them. Perhaps you could give some thought to that by Thursday, because there are 20-odd witnesses. We've had quite a lot of evidence about Dubrovnik. The other matter is one other I've noted which I think we've dealt with, and perhaps you could help me. It's B-1732, and it's Mr. Doyle or -- he may be an army officer. You mentioned something about, and I'm afraid it slipped my memory as to what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We actually have withdrawn our request for the time being because the witness will be called in the Bosnia case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We'll then deal with those at a convenient time on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a comment, a general comment with a specific example. What does 92 bis mean? Look here, the witness who has just got up and who will continue testifying tomorrow is a 92 bis witness, and here five binders have been put on the table relating to her testimony. There is no doubt that 92 bis is being used exclusively to introduce enormous piles of documents which no one can read even theoretically let alone have any kind of serious discussion about them. This cannot be looked at in even a hundred times the time that you have given. It is quite clear that this is simply an attempt to make it impossible to respond to anything delivered in this way, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One practical matter: Is there any dispute that there was this damage to the old town? Is that in dispute at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what's in dispute, Mr. May? What is in fact not indisputable; that Serbia has nothing whatsoever to do with Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, if I may say, is a totally different issue. And if that's the issue we've got to try, let us not spend a lot of time arguing about whether a particular place was damaged or not. If you're not disputing it, then the matter can be dealt with rapidly. Of course there is an issue, as you say, as to whether Serbia or whether you had anything to do with it. That may well be the central issue which we have to decide. It would really clarify things and make things simpler for everybody if we could get on with this evidence with the destruction without having to go into great length about it. But can I say we have in mind the problems which you have with this documentation, that's why I ask you whether there's a dispute about it, and if necessary, you'll have time to look at these things. But as for this particular one, I can't see any great necessity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm not talking only about this particular case. It is the responsibility of the opposite side, on the basis of The Hague Conventions that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff just quoted, using historical monuments to provoke an army, the army of one's own country at that time, and make them shoot. That's what's in dispute; who caused the damage. That is the essential question, although it has nothing to do with Serbia and me. It does concern the JNA, however. The question is was the JNA responsible or the other side which made use of everything that it was not allowed to use in order to provoke this and create a centre for media propaganda in connection with their secession and international recognition. That's what it's about, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying what the particular issues are. Now, as far as these documents are concerned, there doesn't seem to be any prejudice in admitting them. If, however, we come to a time when there's prejudice to you in admitting documents because you haven't had the notice or the time to deal with them properly, you will get the time. Let me clarify something. Wait a moment. Wait a moment. Have these documents been disclosed before, any of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These actually were part of Baca's statement, and they were actually, therefore, all disclosed. What we do here, it was part of -- Ms. Baca's statement were an even bigger amount of exhibits, and we have actually excluded those that are not of interest. And this is why we do this exercise here in a very cursory way, just saying this is a report dealing with the old town, that is a report with the old town, and here is the main report with the old town and we are not going into the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When would it have been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was disclosed in May of last year, but it was also given two days before now in this other fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we've got to finish fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but just a brief question, Mr. May. If I remember well, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you instructed the report to be provided to you by the opposing party regarding the quantity of documents that they are encumbering this whole case with. I don't believe that you have received that report. I haven't seen it. And we still have -- we're still waiting for a reply to the question when you - I'm expecting your answer to that question - when you imagine it is possible to read those hundreds of thousands of pages that have been produced so far, thousands of videotapes and thousands of audiotapes. When do you feel this can be done and how long this should take?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it this way: First of all, in relation to the -- any statements which are admitted under Rule 92 bis, we will ensure that you're not taken by surprise and that you have adequate time to prepare. And if there are a lot of exhibits -- I don't anticipate that there are many exhibits attached to these statements, from what I recollect of them. They're mainly straightforward statements. I'm grateful to the registrar who has given me the report which the Prosecution have produced dated the 12th of February. You should have a copy of that. It's Registry page 19564, so you can find that. And in due course, we'll deal with it. We haven't at the moment dealt with it. There are other matters which we are dealing with, but we have this under consideration. But you might like to find it. As I say, it's 12th of February. Now we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
